title: Tropical Storm Isaias Takes Aim at Gulf Coast as Season's First Hurricane
excerpt: Tropical Storm Isaias formed Wednesday in the Gulf of Mexico with 50 mph winds and is forecast to strengthen into a Category 2 hurricane before landfall Friday night or Saturday along the Mississippi, Alabama or Florida panhandle coast.
body:
• Tropical Storm Isaias formed Wednesday in the Gulf of Mexico — the ninth named storm of the 2026 Atlantic season and the first expected to become a hurricane. At 2 p.m. ET it sat about 520 miles south-southwest of the mouth of the Mississippi River with 50 mph winds.
  • The NHC forecasts Isaias to become a hurricane Thursday and a Category 2 with 110 mph winds Friday, making landfall late Friday or early Saturday along the Mississippi, Alabama or Florida panhandle coast — "looking more likely" to be "a significant hurricane when it reaches the coast."
  • A hurricane watch is in effect from Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, to Indian Pass, Florida, and a storm surge watch from the mouth of the Mississippi River to Yankeetown, Florida. Surge of 5-7 feet is possible from Ocean Springs to Indian Pass plus Mobile Bay; isolated rainfall of up to 10-12 inches could fall across the Gulf Coast, and tropical-storm-force winds arrive by Friday afternoon. Florida has declared a state of emergency in 25 counties — stock kits, fuel or charge vehicles, and check on neighbors now.
  • Isaias would be the latest-forming first hurricane of the Atlantic season since Oct. 8, 1905 — a 121-year record. About 11.2 million barrels of Gulf oil production sit in the storm's path, and U.S. natural gas futures rose 2% Wednesday on supply worries.

Tropical Storm Isaias formed in the Gulf of Mexico on Wednesday and is forecast to strengthen into a hurricane before slamming into the southern U.S. coast late Friday or early Saturday, the National Hurricane Center said — the first hurricane of an Atlantic season already notable for its late start.

As of 2 p.m. ET Wednesday, Isaias sat about 520 miles south-southwest of the mouth of the Mississippi River with 50 mph winds. It should become a hurricane Thursday over warm Gulf waters, intensify to a Category 2 with 110 mph winds Friday, then make landfall — most likely along the Mississippi, Alabama or Florida panhandle coast.

Watches up across the Gulf

The NHC issued a hurricane watch from Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, to Indian Pass, Florida, and a storm surge watch from the mouth of the Mississippi River to Yankeetown, Florida. Surge is the deadliest hazard: 5 to 7 feet of inundation is possible from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, to Indian Pass and across Mobile Bay, with 2 to 4 feet down to Yankeetown.

"We are expecting multiple dangerous, life-threatening impacts along portions of the northern Gulf coast on Friday."

— Mike Brennan, director, National Hurricane Center

Rainfall is the second punch: isolated 10-inch totals from Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle, with AccuWeather putting the heaviest band at 8 to 12 inches across southern Alabama and Mississippi and "flash and urban flooding" possible across the Southeast. NOAA's Storm Prediction Center also flagged tornado potential along the north-central Gulf Coast into early Saturday.

An uncertain track, a record season

The landfall point is not yet pinned down — models have been "somewhat split," the NHC noted, with the official forecast between Gulf Shores, Alabama, and Pensacola, Florida. Rising vertical wind shear in the final 24 hours could weaken the storm, but the NHC still expects a significant hurricane at the coast.

Isaias is already historic: a Thursday upgrade would make it the latest-forming first hurricane of an Atlantic season since Oct. 8, 1905 — a 121-year record, per the Associated Press. Typical seasons produce about seven hurricanes; this season's first eight named storms never got there.

Preparation underway

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency Tuesday for 25 north Florida counties, from Escambia to Baker, letting the state pre-position generators, fuel, water, food, tarps and sandbags in Tallahassee and Santa Rosa County. The Panhandle is already waterlogged: Apalachicola has seen 11.84 inches of rain this week, including a record-tying 7.49 inches on Monday.

Tyndall Air Force Base, east of Panama City, expected destructive winds within 72 hours, and MacDill near Tampa is receiving evacuating aircraft from Tyndall. NOAA and Air Force Reserve Hurricane Hunters have reconnaissance flights scheduled for Wednesday and Thursday.

The economic footprint is already showing: about 11.2 million barrels of Gulf oil production could be lost — far more than the 7.1 million barrels hit by Tropical Storm Bertha in July, per Earth Science Associates — and U.S. natural gas futures climbed 2% Wednesday. Saturday's No. 2 Georgia at No. 7 Alabama game in Tuscaloosa sits under the projected path, with no schedule change yet; President Donald Trump is scheduled to attend. "I hadn't heard about a hurricane... that's not good," he told reporters, according to Reuters.

Diaspora lens

Gulf Coast metro areas in the warning zone — Mobile, Gulfport, Pensacola, Tallahassee — are home to significant Indian-American communities. The National Weather Service's advice applies to everyone in the cone: finalize plans, stock supplies, fuel or charge vehicles, and check on neighbors now.

What's next

The next 48 hours are the watch window: reconnaissance data will sharpen the landfall forecast, and Friday's 110 mph intensity peak will determine what grade of hurricane arrives late Friday or early Saturday. After landfall the storm should weaken rapidly but carry torrential rain inland — into the Ohio Valley, Kentucky, West Virginia and the Carolinas. Residents from Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle should follow every NHC update; this forecast can still shift.
